title: Can a checker catch every loop?
hook: You decide whether each program stops or runs forever. One of them asks you first.

knows: that programs run and either stop or sometimes loop forever
doesNotKnow: that no program can always tell whether another program will stop (the halting problem)

misconception: With enough cleverness, a program could check any other program for infinite loops.
objective: The learner can explain that a program D which asks a checker H about itself and does the opposite makes both of H's answers wrong, so no checker can be right about every program, while particular programs can still be checked.

claims.text: If H says D halts, D loops forever; if H says D loops forever, D stops. Both of H's answers about D are wrong.
claims.source: Case analysis of D's two branches (Demo.tsx PROGRAMS.D.run); there are only two verdicts and each leads to the opposite behaviour.

claims.text: From any checker H that claims to work on every program, we could build its own D, which asks that H about D and does the opposite; so every such H gets the same trap.
claims.source: Standard diagonal construction: Sipser, Introduction to the Theory of Computation (3rd ed.), Theorem 4.11 and its proof (machine D built from H). The stage simplifies 'D run on its own description' to 'D asks H about D'.

claims.text: Turing proved in 1936 that the halting problem cannot be solved by any program: no checker is right about every program.
claims.source: A. M. Turing, 'On Computable Numbers, with an Application to the Entscheidungsproblem', Proc. London Math. Soc. 2(42), 1936-37. The modern 'halting problem' phrasing is later (often credited to Martin Davis); Sipser Thm 4.11 gives the halting form.

claims.text: Particular programs can be checked: A (print, then stop) halts and B (repeat forever) loops, and a verdict on them can be right.
claims.source: Read off the two programs' code on the stage. Stated narrowly: undecidability is about one checker for all programs, not about any single program.

recall.question: A company sells a tool it says can tell, for any program at all, whether the program will ever finish. What is wrong with the claim?
options: Nothing, given a fast enough computer
No tool can be right about every program
It can only fail on very long programs
recall.why: From such a tool you could build a program that asks the tool about itself and does the opposite, so the tool must be wrong somewhere. Particular programs can be checked; all programs cannot.
